articles.headline: The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, and Its Officers
articles.author: H. Harrison Wayman
articles.summary: The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia was organized October the 25th, 1897. It was formed for the object of collecting relics, literature and historical facts relative to the Negro race, illustrating their progress and development in this country. In the Parish building of the Church of the Crucifixion, where the society was organized and meets, a valuable collection is accumulating of rare books, newspapers, pamphlets, clippings and pictures.

events.name: American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia: officers and members named in 1903
events.location: Parish building, Church of the Crucifixion, Philadelphia
events.description: The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia was organized on October 25, 1897, in the Parish building of the Church of the Crucifixion, where it met on the fourth Tuesday of each month. It was formed to collect relics, literature and historical facts about the race. In February 1903 H. Harrison Wayman printed its roll, with sketches and portraits of its six officers, in the Colored American Magazine of Boston. This is a different publication from the Colored American newspaper of 1837-41. Photograph of the Parish building: clippings/CAM_1903-02_p293_church-of-the-crucifixion-parish-building.jpg || Officers in 1903: Robert Mara Adger, president; Theophilus J. Minton, vice-president; Rev. Henry L. Phillips, treasurer; Thomas Herbert Ringgold, corresponding secretary; Edward F. Harris, recording secretary; William Henry Dorsey, custodian. Each officer has a separate entry with his sketch and portrait. || The roll as printed: 'Robert M. Adger, Rev. Henry L. Phillips, pastor of Crucifixion P. E. Church; Rev. Matthew Anderson, pastor of Berean Presbyterian Church; Abel P. Caldwell, managing editor American Herald; Carl Bolivar, a newspaper correspondent; Alfred Cassey, a carver in wood; William H. Dorsey, the artist; Charles H. Brooks, secretary of the G. U. O. O. F.; Walter P. Hall, a produce dealer; Robert Jones, the author; Edward F. Harris, William Potter, Theophilus J. Minton, lawyer; Thomas H. Ringgold, a clerk in the United States postal service; Mr. Hans Shadd, Mr. George Garnett, Mrs. Henry L. Phillips, Mrs. F. E. W. Harper, the celebrated poetess, lecturer, traveller (a sketch of her appeared in the April, 1902, COLORED AMERICAN MAGAZINE); Miss Mary Harper, daughter of Mrs. F. E. W. Harper, an accomplished elocutionist, and Miss Dora Cole, one of Philadelphia's leading educators.' || Wayman adds that the society holds monthly meetings for the reading and discussion of papers, that all persons are eligible to membership regardless of sex, and that it has published a number of pamphlets. || Source: H. Harrison Wayman, 'The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, and Its Officers,' The Colored American Magazine (Boston), vol. 6, no. 4, February 1903, pp. 287-294. events.name: Sketch and portrait of Robert Mara Adger, president of the American Negro Historical Society (1903)
events.description: Robert Mara Adger was born in Charleston, S. C., in 1837, the son of Robert Adger, a Philadelphia merchant for fifty years. In 1903 he was one of six surviving members of the Banneker Institute (printed 'Bannaker'), had helped organize the Fraternal Society in 1860, and had worked in the Philadelphia post office for twenty-one years. He gave more than two hundred portraits and books to the Home for Aged and Infirm Colored Persons, kept there as the Adger Repository. The portrait caption prints his name as 'Robert Marat Adger'. Portrait: clippings/CAM_1903-02_p290_robert-m-adger-portrait.jpg || The sketch as printed: 'Robert Mara Adger, President of the American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, was born in Charleston, S. C., in 1837. Mr. Adger belongs to a very old family; his father, Robert Adger, was a merchant in Philadelphia for fifty years. Mr. Adger is one of the six surviving members of the Bannaker Institute, a famous organization named after Benjamin Bannaker, the Negro astronomer. The members of this old organization have made more individual fame than any other organization of its kind. Mr. Adger was one of the organizers of the Fraternal Society in 1860, which was organized by refugees from South Carolina. In 1873 he was on the staff of General Louis Wagner with the rank of major. Mr. Adger made a collection of over two hundred portraits and books which he was twenty years collecting, and presented them to the Home for Aged and Infirm Colored Persons at Philadelphia. They are now in a room called the Adger Repository. He still has a very interesting collection; among his most valued treasures are some manuscript music compositions by Frank Johnson, the great colored musician. Mr. Adger has been employed in the post office at Philadelphia for twenty-one years, during which time he has filled some very important positions.' || Source: H. Harrison Wayman, 'The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, and Its Officers,' The Colored American Magazine (Boston), vol. 6, no. 4, February 1903, pp. 287-294. Scan: The Digital Colored American Magazine, from the copy in the James Weldon Johnson Memorial Collection, Beinecke Library, Yale: https://coloredamerican.org/?page_id=773

events.name: Sketch and portrait of Theophilus J. Minton, vice-president of the American Negro Historical Society (1903)
events.description: Theophilus J. Minton was born in Philadelphia, read law with Robert B. Elliott of South Carolina, and graduated from the law department of the University of South Carolina. He held a clerkship in the United States Treasury Department, and from 1887 practiced civil law at the Philadelphia Bar. He was a son-in-law of Col. John McKee and represented the family in the contest over McKee's will. Portrait: clippings/CAM_1903-02_p291_theophilus-j-minton-portrait.jpg || The sketch as printed: 'Lawyer Theophilus J. Minton, vice-president A. N. H. S., was born in the city of Philadelphia. Received an academic education and read law with Hon. Robert B. Elliott of South Carolina. Graduated from the law department of the University of South Carolina at Columbia. Appointed by competitive to a clerkship of the United States treasury department at Washington, D. C., where he was promoted by the same means. As a result was chairman of sub-board of law examiners of the United States Civil Service Commissioners in 1881. While in office Mr. Minton prepared a number of decisions involving large amounts of money and important principles of law. In the published reports of the decisions of that office, Lawyer Minton's work has been acknowledged as having been one of a few who had that honor. Since 1887 Lawyer Minton has been in active practice at the Philadelphia Bar, which practice has been entirely confined to civil cases. He is the solicitor of the most important corporation among the colored people of Philadelphia. In 1888 Mr. Minton defended the Philadelphia Amateur Dramatic Company against Peter Reuter, proprietor of Wheatley Dramatic Hall, for breach of contract, on color line. At that time a local reporter described him thus: "A natty young lawyer named Minton, wearing a delicate moustache and equally delicate side whiskers, represented the plaintiffs and represented them well." When the will of Col. John McKee of Philadelphia was announced it was a great shock and surprise to the community. By the provisions of the will the entire estate, with the exception of a few unimportant legacies to his children and grandchildren was given to the Catholic church. Col. McKee being a Presbyterian, the will was contested by his family. The estate was reported to be worth four million dollars. There were a thousand acres of coal and oil lands in West Virginia and Kentucky, and four hundred houses in Philadelphia included. Lawyer Minton was a son-in-law of Col. McKee and represented the family in the contest, while the Catholic side was represented by G. Johnson, and the McKee side by ex-Judge J. G. Gordon, two very eminent white lawyers. The will was settled by compromise.' || Source: H. Harrison Wayman, 'The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, and Its Officers,' The Colored American Magazine (Boston), vol. 6, no. 4, February 1903, pp. 287-294. Scan: The Digital Colored American Magazine, from the copy in the James Weldon Johnson Memorial Collection, Beinecke Library, Yale: https://coloredamerican.org/?page_id=773

events.name: Sketch and portrait of Rev. Henry L. Phillips, treasurer of the American Negro Historical Society (1903)
events.description: Rev. Henry L. Phillips was born in Jamaica, taught school in St. Croix, came to America in 1870 and studied at the Divinity School of the Protestant Episcopal Church in Philadelphia. He was ordained in 1876 and went to the Church of the Crucifixion in 1877. The sketch lists his civic posts, among them trustee of the Theodore Starr Savings Bank and member of the Starr Garden Association. Portrait: clippings/CAM_1903-02_p291_henry-l-phillips-portrait.jpg || The sketch as printed: 'Rev. Henry L. Phillips, the treasurer of the A. N. H. S., was born in Jamaica, B. W. I., studied for a teacher in the Moravian Training School. Taught school in St. Croix, D. W. I. In 1870 he came to America and studied at the Divinity School of the P. E. church at Philadelphia, Pa. In 1876 he was ordained to the priesthood. In 1877 he went to Crucifixion P. E. Church where he has been successfully ministering for twenty-four years. The present church and parish house are the result of his energy. Rev. Phillips is a man of great discretion, his prestige never varies. Among the civic institutions and organizations he is an active member of the Municipal League, a member of the board of managers, The Civil Service Reform League, The Political and Social Science Association, manager of the Law and Order Society, trustee of the Theodore Starr Savings Bank, trustee of the Berean M. I. and I. School, member of the Starr Garden Association and an Odd Fellow. Rev. Phillips is the proper man who keeps himself in the proper place. It is a pity there are so few leaders of his type. Rev. Henry L. Phillips during the spring of 1901 spent a very pleasant time on the Island of Bermuda. Recently the Church of the Crucifixion burned down, including a portion of the parish building. By his influence and energy it has been restored and enlarged. He has been the recipient of many testimonials from friends and his congregation, by whom he is beloved.' || Source: H. Harrison Wayman, 'The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, and Its Officers,' The Colored American Magazine (Boston), vol. 6, no. 4, February 1903, pp. 287-294. Scan: The Digital Colored American Magazine, from the copy in the James Weldon Johnson Memorial Collection, Beinecke Library, Yale: https://coloredamerican.org/?page_id=773

events.name: Sketch and portrait of Thomas Herbert Ringgold, corresponding secretary of the American Negro Historical Society (1903)
events.description: Thomas Herbert Ringgold was born in Port Deposit, Md., in 1864, the son of a grocer there. In Philadelphia he was a messenger in the office of the general manager of the Pennsylvania Railroad, an organizer of the P. R. R. Messengers' Association, and in 1903 a clerk in charge of a United States mail car. Portrait: clippings/CAM_1903-02_p294_thomas-h-ringgold-portrait.jpg || The sketch as printed: 'Thomas Herbert Ringgold, the corresponding secretary of the A. N. H. S., was born in Port Deposit, Md., 1864. Mr. Ringgold's father was a wholesale and retail grocer in that picturesque place for forty-nine years. Mr. Ringgold early adopted Philadelphia as his home. For a number of years he was messenger in the office of Charles Pugh, general manager of the Pennsylvania Railroad. Mr. Ringgold was one of the organizers of the P. R. R. Messengers' Association, an organization which has three thousand dollars to its credit. For a time he was in business trading in produce, etc., as Ringgold Bros. At present Mr. Ringgold is a clerk in charge of one of the United States mail cars in the local service. Among his progressive inclinations he is a devotee of fine art and literature. Mr. Ringgold is an active church worker and a champion of the race.' || Source: H. Harrison Wayman, 'The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, and Its Officers,' The Colored American Magazine (Boston), vol. 6, no. 4, February 1903, pp. 287-294. Scan: The Digital Colored American Magazine, from the copy in the James Weldon Johnson Memorial Collection, Beinecke Library, Yale: https://coloredamerican.org/?page_id=773

events.name: Sketch and portrait of Edward F. Harris, recording secretary of the American Negro Historical Society (1903)
events.description: Edward F. Harris was a native of Philadelphia who attended the school of James Byrd on Sixth Street. He enrolled in Company H, Thirty-second United States Colored Troops, organized at Camp William Penn in March 1864, rose to sergeant, and was wounded at James Island, S. C. After the war he helped organize the John W. Jackson Post, No. 27, G. A. R., in 1867 and was its commander in 1903. Portrait: clippings/CAM_1903-02_p292_edward-f-harris-portrait.jpg || The sketch as printed: 'Edward F. Harris, the recording secretary of the A. N. H. S., is a native of Philadelphia. He attended the renowned school of James Byrd on Sixth street. While only sixteen years of age he was one of the active spirits in organizing Colonel Frismuth's proposed regiment in 1863. Although disappointed, he was a young patriot. He was enrolled in Company H, Thirty-second United States colored troops, which was organized at Camp William Penn, March, 1864. Camp William Penn was on the suburbs of Philadelphia. Mr. Harris soon rose from the ranks to sergeant, and for one day was in charge of fifteen hundred encamped troops. At the front he devoted himself so well as to merit the approval and praise of his company's officers. During the last six weeks of the war he was the acting orderly sergeant in his company, the highest he could go, no matter how worthy. The gallant Thirty-second was sent from Camp William Penn to Hilton Head, S. C., where they arrived in April, 1864. Colonel George W. Baird commanded the regiment, which was on duty near Charleston. The Twenty-second was placed in Advance of the intrenchments. Later in operations on Folly and Morris Islands, Mr. Harris had many narrow escapes. He was in the battles of Honey Hill, S. C., Devereaux Neck, S. C., James Island, S. C., where he was wounded in the thigh, Pocataligo, S. C., Sumterville and Manchester. After the war Harris was identified for a time with the National Guard of Pennsylvania as adjutant of the Thirteenth regiment with the rank of first lieutenant. He helped organize the John W. Jackson Post, 27, G. A. R., in 1867. He has filled every office in it, except two. He is the present commander of the Post, which office he has held for six terms. Mr. Harris was hospital steward under United State Surgeon Wakefield in 1865 for four months. He was presented with a watch as testimonial of service during the great fire at Cape May in 1868. Mr. Harris is well read. He is a Chautauquan and is a member of the Society of the Hall and the Grove and Liberal Arts. Attended the Franklin Institute for two terms. Received a diploma for freehand drawing from the Quaker City fair. Mr. Harris is at present employed by a large mercantile concern.' || Source: H. Harrison Wayman, 'The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, and Its Officers,' The Colored American Magazine (Boston), vol. 6, no. 4, February 1903, pp. 287-294. Scan: The Digital Colored American Magazine, from the copy in the James Weldon Johnson Memorial Collection, Beinecke Library, Yale: https://coloredamerican.org/?page_id=773

events.name: Sketch and portrait of William Henry Dorsey, custodian of the American Negro Historical Society (1903)
events.description: William Henry Dorsey was born in Philadelphia in 1837, the son of one of the three leading caterers of the day. He attended Bird's School and the Institute for Colored Youth and studied art under 'Azeno Schindler'. In 1903 he lived at 206 Dean Street, where three rooms held his museum of books, clippings, pictures and relics, the work of forty years. The caption prints his name as 'W. H. Dorsey'. Portrait: clippings/CAM_1903-02_p294_william-h-dorsey-portrait.jpg || The sketch as printed: 'William Henry Dorsey, custodian of the A. N. H. S., artist, bibliophile, litterateur, numismatist, authority on ceramics, traveller and philanthropist, was born in Philadelphia in 1837; his father was one of the three leading caterers of the day. Mr. Dorsey attended Bird's School and the Institute for Colored Youths, studied art under Azeno Schindler, an Austrian of no mean degree of merit. Mr. Dorsey in public life has filled two positions, first as turnkey at the old central station, afterwards as Mayor Stakley's messenger. Since he held those positions he has devoted his time to his museum, which is without exception the most remarkable collection of books, data, clippings, and curios concerning the Negro race in the world. Mr. Dorsey lives at 206 Dean street, Philadelphia, in one of the houses belonging to his father's estate at whose death it was valued at $60,000. The three rooms devoted to this museum are filled with books, autographs, pictures, ceramics and trophies. These rooms contain the result of forty years' labor. The paintings of John Chapman, the celebrated colored artist of Lear, Socrates, Macbeth and Toussaint L'Overture are fine specimens of that great artist's skill. Mr. Dorsey has a Bannaker Almanac of 1795, band cap of Frank Johnson, the Sousa of the past, five hundred scrap-books of murder stories, rare coins, rare Indian relics, odds and ends which some day will be of infinite service to the city, yes, of the enlightened world.' || Source: H. Harrison Wayman, 'The American Negro Historical Society of Philadelphia, and Its Officers,' The Colored American Magazine (Boston), vol. 6, no. 4, February 1903, pp. 287-294.
